Highest priority

Review cluster-admin grant on ServiceAccount workers/cicd-deployer

If a pod holding this token is compromised, the blast radius is the whole cluster: read every Secret, run privileged workloads, erase the evidence. Confirm the workload genuinely needs cluster-wide write before keeping the grant.

Scope & methodology

1 collector ran in 0s against a single snapshot of acme-pay-prod.

What was examined, the data sources behind every figure, and the assumptions and confidence ranges the conclusions rest on. Read this before the findings.

What this reading could not see

  • ·secrets, configmaps, env valuesnever readdeliberate: this audit does not read a value that could be a credential
  • ·kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease, local-path-storagenot evaluateddeliberate: the components there run privileged by design, so most rules skip what runs in them; rerun with --include-system to evaluate them
  • ·27 resource kindsall readno list this run asked for was refused
  • ·spot vs on-demandknown 12/12every node's purchase mode was read
  • !usagemetrics.k8s.io · instant · shortthe usage window is short, so every consumption figure carries wider uncertainty than the method asks for

Collectors & data sources

Collectors run: kubernetes

  • Kubernetes API (server v1.31.2-eks-1a2b3c4)
  • Pricing: AWS on-demand list (as of 2026-09, embedded); no discount applied — confirm against your RI/Savings-Plan rates (a commitment covers compute hours only; storage, load balancers and control-plane fees are list either way). Persistent-volume storage summed from PV/PVC capacity at list per GB-month
  • 1 unpriced storage class(es) excluded from storage spend: (no storageClass)
  • Usage: metrics.k8s.io (window instant) — 28 container series — caveats: metrics.k8s.io is an instantaneous snapshot — not a windowed p95
  • Stack CRDs: read via dynamic discovery (status/spec only, no secrets) as of 2026-09-15

Compliance coverage ceiling: Shoalcheck is a read-only Kubernetes API client, so it machine-checks the cluster-observable policy layer — 28 of the 32 controls in CIS Kubernetes Benchmark v1.9 (Section 5 subset) have an automated check in this build (RBAC, workload securityContext, NetworkPolicies, namespace PSA labels), scored here over 28 machine-checked controls. Control-plane, etcd, and worker-node controls (CIS Sections 1–4) are provider-managed on EKS/AKS/GKE and not assessable from a read-only API client — they are reported as "Not assessed", never pass/fail. Container-field checks read the spec as authored; the PodSecurity admission check (rule k8s.namespace.pss-admission-not-enforced) reports what the cluster actually enforces. SOC2/PCI/NSA-CISA rows are evidence-pointers, not a self-scored coverage claim.

Rule versions and collector provenance are recorded per finding. This document is a point-in-time snapshot; re-run the audit to refresh. The pricing basis, assumptions and footnotes behind every derived figure are itemised in the Appendix.

Status of this report & limitations

This report contains observations and potential gaps, mapped to control frameworks (PCI-DSS, SOC 2, CIS) for convenience. It is not a certified audit and is not issued by a QSA, CPA, or accredited auditor. Nothing here constitutes an audit opinion, certification, or attestation.

Compliance references are indicators for further review, not pass/fail attestations. A control mapped to a finding flags an area to examine with your QSA or auditor; it does not assert compliance or non-compliance. Failed checks read as "potential gap", never "violation".

Findings are generated from a point-in-time, read-only API snapshot of the cluster (plus optional Prometheus metrics). They reflect the cluster as observed at the audit date and require human validation before any action is taken.

This report is provided with no warranty, express or implied. The operator is responsible for independently verifying every remediation in a non-production environment before applying it to production systems.

Findings

1 critical and 11 high-severity findings lead 137 total — address the Critical group first.

137 findings across 64 issue types, presented Critical-first. Each card follows one fixed schema — what it is, the business impact, the evidence, and the remediation. Use the filters or the by-type rollup to narrow.

Start here 3 of 137 findings

Ranked by consequence, then by what is safely actionable. The full list is unchanged below — this is a lens over it, not a filter.

  1. 1

    No ready address is published for api/api-gateway +3 more of the same rule

    true now · 4 resources across 2 namespaces · no mechanical remediation — needs a person · under 30 minutes · Only the cluster's own controllers can report the published set, and a zero there is invisible to a deployment that reported success — this is the reading worth confirming against what the Service is meant to do.

    manual

  2. 2

    Deployment api/api-gateway runs 2 different builds of registry.acme.example/api-gateway:latest

    true now · 2 resources · no mechanical remediation — needs a person · under 30 minutes · Every replica reads as identical in every manifest and in every dashboard that shows the tag, so the difference is invisible from everywhere except the pod status

    manual

  3. 3

    Deployment default/legacy-cron-runner has a container restarted 37 times

    true now · 1 resource · no mechanical remediation — needs a person · A container that keeps being restarted is being kept alive by the kubelet rather than by working, and each restart drops whatever was in memory

    manual

Safest place to begin: Single replica without PDB: default/legacy-cron-runner — its remediation is additive and does not restart workloads.

Right-size over-provisioned requests on api/api-gateway

Deployment api/api-gateway

Description

Deployment api/api-gateway reserves CPU/memory above what its instant usage ever needed, across 2 replica(s). CPU is sized to the busiest replica's p95 plus 30% headroom; memory to the larger of p95×1.3 and the observed instant max. The memory recommendation is floored at the observed instant max so a bursty or GC-heavy workload is not down-sized below a working set it provably reaches. This reclaims reserved capacity the workload's instant p95 never used — but the 95th percentile excludes tail bursts, so verify against the container's instant max and your latency SLOs before applying: CPU below request is throttled, memory below peak is OOMKilled.

Business impact

Requests far above real usage reserve node capacity nothing consumes, inflating the cluster's node count and bill.

Estimated $25/mo ($300/yr) at on-demand list pricing.

Evidence (6)
  • container api-gateway in Deployment api/api-gateway: requests 500m CPU, instant p95 usage 160m (×1.3 headroom = 209m) -> recommend 210m, reclaim 290m × 2 replicas; requests 1024Mi mem, instant p95 usage 348Mi / instant max 593Mi (recommend = max(p95×1.3, max×1.05), recommend floored at instant max = 624Mi), reclaim 400Mi × 2 replicas
  • $ model (UPPER BOUND, if consolidated): reclaim 580m CPU / 800Mi mem across 2 replica(s), divided by m6i.xlarge allocatable (3900m CPU / 15360Mi) × $167.90/node/mo (eu-central-1) -> CPU-bound up to $24.97/mo
  • $ scaled by 2 replica(s) (declared spec replicas)
  • realisation caveat: reclaimed requests convert to a real bill reduction only if the cluster is node-count-bound on the freed dimension AND an autoscaler/manual pool-shrink removes a node; on a memory-bound or fixed-size pool, freeing CPU saves $0 until the pool shrinks
  • data-quality: the figures above rest on instant of history, as the usage source reported it; a shorter window biases a p95 toward the quiet hours it happened to cover
  • data-quality: observed instant memory MAX is well above p95 (bursty/GC-heavy) — the recommendation is floored at the max, but p95 alone would have under-sized it
What this does not establish (5)
  • The figure is computed from a dated public list price, not from your bill. No credential of yours was used and no invoice was read, so a negotiated rate, a private offer or a credit is invisible here.
  • Whether a commitment already covers this footprint is a billing-account fact this product cannot see. A saving stated at the on-demand rate is wrong for the term of any plan that already applies.
  • Identified is not realised. Nothing here has been reclaimed, and the arithmetic assumes the freed capacity is actually given up rather than absorbed elsewhere.
  • This rests on a measured window from a metrics source, so it is only as long as that source has been running: a young Prometheus reports a short window and the confidence says so. Without a usage source the rule emits nothing rather than guessing.
  • Requests are compared against observed p95 with headroom, taking the busiest replica rather than the mean. It is a statement about reserved capacity, never about whether the workload is fast enough.
Affected resources (1)
  • Deployment api/api-gateway
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
  namespace: api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api-gateway
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 210m      # instant p95 ×1.3, right-sized
              memory: 624Mi  # instant p95 ×1.3, right-sized

Drop ALL capabilities then add back only what api/api-gateway needs

Deployment api/api-gateway

Description

Deployment api/api-gateway has 1 of 1 container(s) that do not drop ALL capabilities, so each keeps the default Linux capability set (NET_RAW included). The PSS-Restricted profile requires capabilities.drop:[ALL]; add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE if the container binds a privileged port. This reads the spec AS AUTHORED, not as admitted: a PodSecurity admission profile or mutating webhook could reject or fill this field at admission time. Read alongside the namespace's PodSecurity admission level (k8s.namespace.pss-admission-not-enforced) to know whether the cluster actually enforces it.

Business impact

Containers keep a default capability set (including NET_RAW) unless they explicitly drop ALL — a wide kernel surface most apps never use.

A probe on Deployment api/api-gateway targets an undeclared port

Deployment api/api-gateway

Description

Deployment api/api-gateway has a probe whose port matches no containerPort declared on the same container. The container DOES declare ports, which is what makes the mismatch readable: the spec names one set of ports and probes a different one.

Business impact

A probe and a port declaration that name different things are two halves of one intention, written at different times. Whether the port the probe names is the one the process listens on is outside this reading — which is exactly why the disagreement is worth surfacing rather than resolving: it is the kind of mismatch that survives review, because both numbers look plausible beside each other.

Evidence (4)
  • Snapshot taken at 2026-09-15T05:28:50Z. Each resource kind is listed independently, so the node, pod and budget views can differ by moments; re-verify against the live cluster before acting.
  • container api-gateway in Deployment api/api-gateway: livenessProbe targets port 8080, and this container declares no such containerPort (it declares: "web"/9090)
  • container api-gateway in Deployment api/api-gateway: readinessProbe targets port 8080, and this container declares no such containerPort (it declares: "web"/9090)
  • containerPort is documentation rather than a binding — a process may listen on a port it never declared — so what is reported here is the spec disagreeing with itself, and nothing about the outcome
What this does not establish (3)
  • The finding is that the reference resolves to nothing in this reading. It is not a prediction of what will happen: a pod created after the target went away behaves differently from one that has been running for a month on a token it already holds, and the snapshot cannot tell which it is looking at.
  • This is an absence claim over the TARGET list, so it is made only when that list was actually read. A refused list produces silence here rather than a cluster that appears entirely broken.
  • Kinds this product does not collect are excluded and counted, never reported as missing — an autoscaler may target an Argo Rollout or a KEDA ScaledObject, and calling those absent would fire on every cluster running one.

Enforce non-root at the API for api/api-gateway (runAsNonRoot unset)

Deployment api/api-gateway

Description

Deployment api/api-gateway does not enforce non-root execution at the API in 1 of 1 container(s): runAsNonRoot is unset and no non-zero runAsUser is set. The container image's USER directive is invisible to a read-only API client, so an unset spec is reported as UNCONFIRMED non-root, never "runs as root" — and rated Medium, like the other PSS fields a spec can leave unset. It is rated High only when root is confirmed or near-certain: an explicit runAsUser:0 / runAsNonRoot:false, or a known root-by-default base image with no non-root assertion (each called out per container in the evidence). Set runAsNonRoot:true (and a non-zero runAsUser) on the pod or container securityContext to make non-root intent explicit and admission-enforceable. This reads the spec AS AUTHORED, not as admitted: a PodSecurity admission profile or mutating webhook could reject or fill this field at admission time. Read alongside the namespace's PodSecurity admission level (k8s.namespace.pss-admission-not-enforced) to know whether the cluster actually enforces it.

Business impact

A container that does not assert non-root may run as UID 0, so a container escape inherits root on the node instead of an unprivileged user.

Pin mutable image references on api/api-gateway

Deployment api/api-gateway

Description

Deployment api/api-gateway has 1 image reference(s) that can resolve to different bytes on different pulls. The same manifest may then run different code across nodes or after a restart, which breaks rollbacks and makes incident forensics guesswork. Pin a specific version tag or, for true immutability, a digest (@sha256:…). On a genuinely fixed tag, imagePullPolicy=IfNotPresent is then safe.

Business impact

Mutable image references make deploys non-reproducible — during an incident, 'what exactly is running' becomes harder to answer. (A digest-pinned image passes here even if it also carries a :latest tag; the digest, not the tag, fixes the bytes.)

Disable default SA token automount on api/api-gateway

Deployment api/api-gateway

Description

Deployment api/api-gateway sets no dedicated ServiceAccount and mounts the default SA's API token into every container. No RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding observed in this cluster references this namespace's default SA, so the token grants only baseline authenticated/discovery access today — but any future RoleBinding silently widens this exposure to every pod already on the default SA. If this workload does need API access, give it a dedicated ServiceAccount with a scoped Role instead. Exception: if this pod uses the projected token for cloud IAM (EKS IRSA / Pod Identity, GKE Workload Identity), disabling automount will break that — give it a dedicated SA configured for the integration instead of turning the token off.

Business impact

A mounted token is an unnecessary credential surface: it costs nothing to remove and prevents a future RBAC grant from silently turning every default-SA pod into an authenticated API client.

Evidence (2)
  • Deployment api/api-gateway runs as default SA with token automounted
  • no Role/ClusterRole binding observed references the default SA in api (baseline authenticated access only)
What this does not establish (2)
  • This is read from the workload's declared pod template, not from what is running. Admission may inject or mutate containers, so the pod the scheduler placed is not always the pod described here.
  • A declared setting is not a demonstrated behaviour. Nothing here says this workload behaved in any particular way, only what its specification declares.
Affected resources (1)
  • Deployment api/api-gateway
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# Validate before applying: if this pod relies on a projected token for
# cloud IAM (EKS IRSA / Pod Identity, GKE Workload Identity) or actually
# calls the Kubernetes API, do NOT disable automount — give it a dedicated
# ServiceAccount configured for that integration instead.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
  namespace: api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      automountServiceAccountToken: false

  • realisation caveat: reclaimed requests convert to a real bill reduction only if the cluster is node-count-bound on the freed dimension AND an autoscaler/manual pool-shrink removes a node; on a memory-bound or fixed-size pool, freeing CPU saves $0 until the pool shrinks
  • data-quality: the figures above rest on instant of history, as the usage source reported it; a shorter window biases a p95 toward the quiet hours it happened to cover
  • data-quality: observed instant memory MAX is well above p95 (bursty/GC-heavy) — the recommendation is floored at the max, but p95 alone would have under-sized it
What this does not establish (5)
  • The figure is computed from a dated public list price, not from your bill. No credential of yours was used and no invoice was read, so a negotiated rate, a private offer or a credit is invisible here.
  • Whether a commitment already covers this footprint is a billing-account fact this product cannot see. A saving stated at the on-demand rate is wrong for the term of any plan that already applies.
  • Identified is not realised. Nothing here has been reclaimed, and the arithmetic assumes the freed capacity is actually given up rather than absorbed elsewhere.
  • This rests on a measured window from a metrics source, so it is only as long as that source has been running: a young Prometheus reports a short window and the confidence says so. Without a usage source the rule emits nothing rather than guessing.
  • Requests are compared against observed p95 with headroom, taking the busiest replica rather than the mean. It is a statement about reserved capacity, never about whether the workload is fast enough.

Deployment api/auth-service

Deployment api/auth-service has 1 of 1 container(s) whose effective seccompProfile is unset or Unconfined (computed pod then container). Set seccompProfile.type:RuntimeDefault at the pod level so every container inherits syscall filtering — required by PSS-Restricted (CIS 5.7.2 maps to 5.2.1 in this benchmark version). This reads the spec AS AUTHORED, not as admitted: a PodSecurity admission profile or mutating webhook could reject or fill this field at admission time. Deployment api/auth-service

Deployment api/auth-service runs 2 replicas but declares no podAntiAffinity and no topologySpreadConstraints. The scheduler may co-locate replicas on one node, so one node failure or drain could take several down together. Observed 12 schedulable node(s) across 3 zone(s).

Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# Validate against your workload before applying: with whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway this is
# soft (won't block scheduling); spread is bounded by the number of schedulable nodes/zones.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: auth-service
  namespace: api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: auth-service

Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# TEMPLATE — do NOT apply blind. A liveness probe configured too aggressively
# (no startupProbe, low failureThreshold, short timeout) will restart healthy-but-slow
# pods and can cascade the whole Deployment into CrashLoopBackOff. Set the real
# health path/port and tune the timings to your workload's warmup + GC behaviour first.
#
# startupProbe gates liveness until the app has finished starting; give slow-start
# apps (JVM, large models, migrations) a generous startup budget.
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: http }   # <-- set to your real health endpoint
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 30                       # ~5 min warmup budget; raise for slow starters
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: http }   # <-- set to your real health endpoint
  periodSeconds: 15
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3

Disable default SA token automount on api/auth-service

Deployment api/auth-service

Description

Deployment api/auth-service sets no dedicated ServiceAccount and mounts the default SA's API token into every container. No RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding observed in this cluster references this namespace's default SA, so the token grants only baseline authenticated/discovery access today — but any future RoleBinding silently widens this exposure to every pod already on the default SA. If this workload does need API access, give it a dedicated ServiceAccount with a scoped Role instead. Exception: if this pod uses the projected token for cloud IAM (EKS IRSA / Pod Identity, GKE Workload Identity), disabling automount will break that — give it a dedicated SA configured for the integration instead of turning the token off.

Business impact

A mounted token is an unnecessary credential surface: it costs nothing to remove and prevents a future RBAC grant from silently turning every default-SA pod into an authenticated API client.

Evidence (2)

  • no Role/ClusterRole binding observed references the default SA in api (baseline authenticated access only)

Affected resources (1)
  • Deployment api/auth-service
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# Validate before applying: if this pod relies on a projected token for
# cloud IAM (EKS IRSA / Pod Identity, GKE Workload Identity) or actually
# calls the Kubernetes API, do NOT disable automount — give it a dedicated
# ServiceAccount configured for that integration instead.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: auth-service
  namespace: api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      automountServiceAccountToken: false

Deployment api/auth-service

A container in Deployment api/auth-service declares the same environment variable name more than once. Kubernetes accepts this and the last one wins, so the earlier value is silently discarded — the manifest reads as though both were set.

Deployment default/legacy-cron-runner sets no dedicated ServiceAccount and mounts the default SA's API token into every container. No RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding observed in this cluster references this namespace's default SA, so the token grants only baseline authenticated/discovery access today — but any future RoleBinding silently widens this exposure to every pod already on the default SA. If this workload does need API access, give it a dedicated ServiceAccount with a scoped Role instead. Exception: if this pod uses the projected token for cloud IAM (EKS IRSA / Pod Identity, GKE Workload Identity), disabling automount will break that — give it a dedicated SA configured for the integration instead of turning the token off.

Business impact

A mounted token is an unnecessary credential surface: it costs nothing to remove and prevents a future RBAC grant from silently turning every default-SA pod into an authenticated API client.

Evidence (2)

Remediation
Apply this manifest

# Validate before applying: if this pod relies on a projected token for
# cloud IAM (EKS IRSA / Pod Identity, GKE Workload Identity) or actually
# calls the Kubernetes API, do NOT disable automount — give it a dedicated
# ServiceAccount configured for that integration instead.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: legacy-cron-runner
  namespace: default
spec:
  template:

# TEMPLATE — do NOT apply blind. A liveness probe configured too aggressively
# (no startupProbe, low failureThreshold, short timeout) will restart healthy-but-slow

Spread monitoring/node-exporter replicas across nodes

Deployment monitoring/node-exporter

Description

Deployment monitoring/node-exporter runs 3 replicas but declares no podAntiAffinity and no topologySpreadConstraints. The scheduler may co-locate replicas on one node, so one node failure or drain could take several down together. Observed 12 schedulable node(s) across 3 zone(s).

Business impact

Replicas co-located on one node die together — without a spread rule the redundancy you pay for may buy less availability than the replica count implies.

Evidence (1)
  • Deployment monitoring/node-exporter: 3 replicas, no podAntiAffinity/topologySpreadConstraints
What this does not establish (2)
  • This is read from the workload's declared pod template, not from what is running. Admission may inject or mutate containers, so the pod the scheduler placed is not always the pod described here.
  • A declared setting is not a demonstrated behaviour. Nothing here says this workload behaved in any particular way, only what its specification declares.
Affected resources (1)
  • Deployment monitoring/node-exporter
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# Validate against your workload before applying: with whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway this is
# soft (won't block scheduling); spread is bounded by the number of schedulable nodes/zones.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: node-exporter
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: node-exporter

Deployment payments/payments-orchestrator reserves CPU/memory above what its instant usage ever needed, across 3 replica(s). Business impact

Requests far above real usage reserve node capacity nothing consumes, inflating the cluster's node count and bill.

  • container payments-orchestrator in Deployment payments/payments-orchestrator: requests 1000m CPU, instant p95 usage 320m (×1.3 headroom = 417m) -> recommend 420m, reclaim 580m × 3 replicas; requests 2048Mi mem, instant p95 usage 696Mi / instant max 1187Mi (recommend = max(p95×1.3, max×1.05), recommend floored at instant max = 1248Mi), reclaim 800Mi × 3 replicas
  • $ model (UPPER BOUND, if consolidated): reclaim 1740m CPU / 2400Mi mem across 3 replica(s), divided by m6i.xlarge allocatable (3900m CPU / 15360Mi) × $167.90/node/mo (eu-central-1) -> CPU-bound up to $74.91/mo
  • $ scaled by 3 replica(s) (declared spec replicas)
  • realisation caveat: reclaimed requests convert to a real bill reduction only if the cluster is node-count-bound on the freed dimension AND an autoscaler/manual pool-shrink removes a node; on a memory-bound or fixed-size pool, freeing CPU saves $0 until the pool shrinks
  • data-quality: the figures above rest on instant of history, as the usage source reported it; a shorter window biases a p95 toward the quiet hours it happened to cover
  • data-quality: observed instant memory MAX is well above p95 (bursty/GC-heavy) — the recommendation is floored at the max, but p95 alone would have under-sized it
What this does not establish (5)

  • This rests on a measured window from a metrics source, so it is only as long as that source has been running: a young Prometheus reports a short window and the confidence says so. Without a usage source the rule emits nothing rather than guessing.

# TEMPLATE — do NOT apply blind. A liveness probe configured too aggressively
# (no startupProbe, low failureThreshold, short timeout) will restart healthy-but-slow
# pods and can cascade the whole Deployment into CrashLoopBackOff. Set the real
# health path/port and tune the timings to your workload's warmup + GC behaviour first.
#
# startupProbe gates liveness until the app has finished starting; give slow-start
# apps (JVM, large models, migrations) a generous startup budget.
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: http }   # <-- set to your real health endpoint
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 30                       # ~5 min warmup budget; raise for slow starters
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: http }   # <-- set to your real health endpoint
  periodSeconds: 15
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3

Secret material reaches payments/payments-gateway through the environment

Deployment payments/payments-gateway

Description

Deployment payments/payments-gateway takes 1 value(s) from 1 Secret(s) (payments-db-credentials) as environment variables. The pod template names the Secret; no Secret was read and no value was seen.

Disable default SA token automount on api/search-indexer

Deployment api/search-indexer

Description

Deployment api/search-indexer sets no dedicated ServiceAccount and mounts the default SA's API token into every container. No RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding observed in this cluster references this namespace's default SA, so the token grants only baseline authenticated/discovery access today — but any future RoleBinding silently widens this exposure to every pod already on the default SA. If this workload does need API access, give it a dedicated ServiceAccount with a scoped Role instead. Exception: if this pod uses the projected token for cloud IAM (EKS IRSA / Pod Identity, GKE Workload Identity), disabling automount will break that — give it a dedicated SA configured for the integration instead of turning the token off.

Business impact

A mounted token is an unnecessary credential surface: it costs nothing to remove and prevents a future RBAC grant from silently turning every default-SA pod into an authenticated API client.

Single replica without PDB: payments/payments-ledger-db

StatefulSet payments/payments-ledger-db

Description

StatefulSet payments/payments-ledger-db runs exactly one replica and no PodDisruptionBudget matches its pods. No Service in the namespace selects its pods on a serving port, so loss of the pod is not directly user-facing — but any node drain or interruption still takes the single replica down until it reschedules. This is a StatefulSet: do NOT simply scale to 2 — verify the application supports >1 replica (replication / quorum) first, or a second replica can corrupt data.

Business impact

No Service fronts this replica on a serving port, so a node event is unlikely to be user-visible — but the workload still vanishes briefly on any drain. For a StatefulSet, confirm the app supports multiple replicas before scaling; only then is a PodDisruptionBudget (on at least 2 replicas) appropriate — a PDB on a single replica blocks every node drain.

Evidence (3)
  • StatefulSet payments/payments-ledger-db: spec.replicas = 1
  • No PodDisruptionBudget in namespace payments selects pod labels map[app:payments-ledger-db]
  • No Service in namespace payments selects these pod labels (workload not directly exposed)
What this does not establish (2)
  • This is read from the workload's declared pod template, not from what is running. Admission may inject or mutate containers, so the pod the scheduler placed is not always the pod described here.
  • A declared setting is not a demonstrated behaviour. Nothing here says this workload behaved in any particular way, only what its specification declares.

  • StatefulSet payments/payments-ledger-db

Review cluster-admin grant on ServiceAccount workers/cicd-deployer

ClusterRoleBinding acme-deployer-cluster-admin

+1 more resource
Description

ClusterRoleBinding acme-deployer-cluster-admin binds the cluster-admin ClusterRole (cluster-wide) to 1 ServiceAccount(s). Every pod running under such an account carries a token with unrestricted API access. The grant itself is a fact; whether it is justified depends on what the workload actually does.

Business impact

If a pod holding this token is compromised, the blast radius is the whole cluster: read every Secret, run privileged workloads, erase the evidence. Confirm the workload genuinely needs cluster-wide write before keeping the grant.

Evidence (2)
  • ClusterRoleBinding acme-deployer-cluster-admin: ServiceAccount workers/cicd-deployer -> cluster-admin
  • scope note: matches the built-in ClusterRole "cluster-admin" by name only — custom wildcard (*,*,*) or aggregated ClusterRoles are functionally equivalent but out of scope (role bodies not collected)
What this does not establish (3)
  • This names one role's rules and the bindings that activate it. It is not a total: a subject's effective permissions are the union over every binding that names it or any group it belongs to, and group membership is decided by the authenticator rather than by anything in the cluster.
  • A permission is not a use. Nothing here says the grant was exercised; the snapshot carries no audit log and no request history.
  • The bindings Kubernetes writes for itself are not counted as activating a role: the label kubernetes.io/bootstrapping: rbac-defaults AND the exact upstream binding — name, role and subjects. The label alone is not trusted. Two upstream bindings are counted anyway, because their roles may have been edited and the API server never removes a permission: one naming a broad group such as system:authenticated, and one whose role grants every verb on every resource and is not cluster-admin. A bootstrap role edited in any narrower way is not detected.
Affected resources (2)
  • ClusterRoleBinding acme-deployer-cluster-admin
  • ServiceAccount workers/cicd-deployer
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# Least-privilege replacement for a cluster-admin grant.
# DO NOT delete the original ClusterRoleBinding until this scoped role is confirmed to cover
# the ServiceAccount's OBSERVED usage — removing it first will break the
# workload. Fill the rules below from what cicd-deployer actually does (audit logs / what
# it watches), then cut over and remove the cluster-admin binding.
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: cicd-deployer-scoped
rules:
  # fill with the verbs this SA actually uses (placeholder below)
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: cicd-deployer-scoped
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cicd-deployer-scoped
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: cicd-deployer
    namespace: workers

ClusterRoleBinding acme-break-glass binds Group system:masters

ClusterRoleBinding acme-break-glass

Description

ClusterRoleBinding acme-break-glass names Group system:masters as a subject and points at ClusterRole cluster-admin, cluster-wide. system:masters is authorized above RBAC: the API server grants its members every action on every resource without consulting any Role, so this binding is a signal that a break-glass path exists rather than the thing that grants the power. This is what the binding says; what any holder of that subject can actually do is the union over every binding that names it, and the absence of a binding is not the absence of the subject: a client certificate carrying O=system:masters, an OIDC claim or a provider IAM mapping makes its holder a member with no RBAC object anywhere.

Business impact

system:masters is authorized above RBAC: the API server grants its members every action on every resource without consulting any Role, so this binding is a signal that a break-glass path exists rather than the thing that grants the power, so a binding that names it hands the referenced role to everyone it covers at once, without any of them appearing in this or any other object.

Evidence (2)
  • ClusterRoleBinding acme-break-glass: subjects include Group system:masters
  • ClusterRoleBinding acme-break-glass: roleRef is ClusterRole cluster-admin, cluster-wide
What this does not establish (5)
  • An absence here is not an absence of the subject. Membership is decided outside the cluster — a client certificate's O=, an OIDC claim, a provider's IAM mapping, or for the unauthenticated identities the simple absence of a credential — so a reading with no such binding has not established that nobody holds it.
  • Whether the grant is reachable was not established. Anonymous requests are accepted or refused by a control-plane flag a managed cluster does not expose, so a binding naming an unauthenticated subject may be live or may be unreachable, and this reading cannot tell those apart.
  • Nothing here is a statement about the role's contents. This finding is about the subject a binding names; what the referenced role permits is a separate reading, and a harmless role bound to a dangerous subject is reported here exactly as a powerful one is.
  • A permission is not a use. Nothing here says the grant was exercised; the snapshot carries no audit log and no request history.
  • The bindings Kubernetes writes for itself are excluded: the label kubernetes.io/bootstrapping: rbac-defaults AND the exact binding the upstream bootstrap policy writes — its name, its role and its subjects, no more and no fewer. The label alone is not trusted, because anybody who can create a binding can set it; a labelled binding that is not the upstream one is reported like any other. A binding an installer created without that label is reported even where it is that installer's normal behaviour, because a rule that decided which installers to trust would be making a judgement this reading cannot support.

A node roll meets 1 of 12 node(s) it cannot evacuate

Node ip-10-0-2-a

Description

A node-image upgrade replaces nodes one at a time, and each replacement needs the node evacuated first. 1 of this cluster's 12 node(s) carry work that this reading finds no remaining node for. Each is already reported on its own; this states what they mean together, which is that the roll does not complete without forcing one of them.

Business impact

A single node that cannot be drained is something an operator can live with indefinitely. An upgrade cannot: it has to visit every node, so the same fact changes from an inconvenience into a stopping condition.

Evidence (5)
  • Snapshot taken at 2026-09-15T05:28:50Z. Each resource kind is listed independently, so the node, pod and budget views can differ by moments; re-verify against the live cluster before acting.
  • 1 of 12 node(s): ip-10-0-2-a
  • each is reported by k8s.reliability.node-loss-feasibility, findings f-44531237a3ea — the evidence is there and is deliberately not repeated here, so one problem is not counted twice
  • no duration, no ordering, and no claim that the upgrade fails: the supportable sentence is that the roll encounters these nodes
  • the managed provider's own upgrade orchestration — surge nodes, batch size, its own eviction handling — is not read and not modelled
What this does not establish (5)
  • This says what the cluster will stop SERVING, never what will break. When a version is removed the existing objects keep being served at the surviving version; what breaks is clients — YAML in a repository, a Helm chart, a controller's library, a CI pipeline — and none of those is inside a kubeconfig.
  • No workload is named as being at risk, deliberately. The object is precisely the thing that survives a version removal, so naming one would assert the opposite of what is true.
  • What is SERVED is not what is APPLIED. `last-applied-configuration` would be the obvious source for the latter and is refused: it is absent on every GitOps cluster, nothing updates it on a storage migration, and it holds the entire applied manifest.
  • A group/version string is not a stable identity across releases — one API was removed in 1.22 and reintroduced in 1.28 — so the removal schedule is read as a dated dataset with a version and a stamp, not as a permanent fact.
  • Silence from this family means these checks ran and found nothing. It is not a statement that the upgrade will succeed.

Cluster 1.31

Description

The cluster reports Kubernetes 1.31. Ordinary support from AWS ended on 2025-11-26; the cluster is inside the paid extension, which ends 2026-11-26.

Business impact

A version past ordinary support is billed at a higher per-cluster rate by EKS and AKS, and nothing inside the cluster says so — the charge appears on an invoice nobody reads beside a version number nobody connected to it.

Estimated $365/mo ($4,380/yr) at on-demand list pricing.

  • published window for AWS 1.31: released 2024-09-26, ordinary support ended 2025-11-26, paid extension ends 2026-11-26
  • AWS bills $0.5000 per cluster-hour on top of the ordinary control-plane rate while a version is in extended support — about $365.00 a month for this cluster, every month until it is upgraded. The figure is the SURCHARGE alone: the ordinary control plane is billed either way, so an upgrade stops this amount and not the whole control-plane bill.
  • support dates are from the reference table fetched 2026-08-31; they are compared against the snapshot's own timestamp, not against today, so re-rendering this collection cannot change the verdict
  • this reading is the version's SUPPORT STATE. Whether an upgrade is safe for this cluster is a different question, and k8s.reliability's upgrade rules are where it is asked

Enforce a PodSecurity admission profile on namespace default

Namespace default

Description

Namespace default runs workloads but does not enforce a PodSecurity admission profile of baseline or restricted (enforce=<unset>). Without enforcement, the per-container PSS findings in this report describe the spec AS AUTHORED — nothing in the cluster actually blocks a privileged, root, or capability-laden pod from being admitted here. Apply the labels gradually: set warn and audit first to surface what would break, then set enforce. Enforcing restricted on a namespace that already runs noncompliant pods does NOT evict them, but it WILL block the next admission (a redeploy or rollout) — stage it. baseline is the safe first target (it blocks privileged, hostPath, hostNetwork, and host namespaces); however, the per-container findings in this report for this namespace (seccomp, drop-ALL capabilities, allowPrivilegeEscalation, runAsNonRoot) are Restricted-profile controls, so enforce=restricted is required to fully close them — baseline alone will not.

Business impact

PodSecurity admission is the only thing that turns securityContext hardening from a suggestion into a guarantee — without it, a single noncompliant manifest re-opens every gap the per-container checks flag.

Evidence (1)
  • namespace default: enforce=<unset>, warn=<unset>, audit=<unset> — admission does not block any pod
What this does not establish (2)
  • This reports what is not configured, which is not the same as what is not enforced. A CNI may carry segmentation in its own policy objects, which this product does not read, so the absence of an upstream NetworkPolicy is not the absence of isolation.
  • An admission control governs what may be applied next. It says nothing about what is already running, which was admitted under whatever policy was in force at the time.
Affected resources (1)
  • Namespace default
Remediation
Run this command
SHELL 
kubectl label --overwrite namespace default pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=baseline pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=baseline   # surface breakage first, then set enforce=baseline; use restricted (not baseline) on both warn/audit/enforce to close the per-container seccomp/capabilities/runAsNonRoot findings

Namespace api has no NetworkPolicy — add a default-deny if its CNI enforces policy

Namespace api

Description

Namespace api runs 3 workload(s) and defines zero upstream (networking.k8s.io/v1) NetworkPolicy objects. Enforcement of NetworkPolicy depends on the cluster CNI, which could not be confirmed here (a NetworkPolicy is accepted by the API server but silently ignored without an enforcing CNI). If the CNI enforces policy, start with a default-deny-ingress policy, then add explicit allows for the flows that exist.

Business impact

If the cluster CNI enforces NetworkPolicy, flat pod-to-pod networking lets a single compromised container move laterally across the namespace. If the CNI does not enforce policy (or segments via its own CRDs), this gap may be theoretical — confirm enforcement before relying on it.

Evidence (2)
  • namespace api: 3 workload(s), 0 networking.k8s.io/v1 NetworkPolicy objects
  • CNI enforcement of NetworkPolicy could not be confirmed from collected DaemonSets — verify the cluster CNI supports and enforces NetworkPolicy before relying on this remediation
What this does not establish (2)
  • This reports what is not configured, which is not the same as what is not enforced. A CNI may carry segmentation in its own policy objects, which this product does not read, so the absence of an upstream NetworkPolicy is not the absence of isolation.
  • An admission control governs what may be applied next. It says nothing about what is already running, which was admitted under whatever policy was in force at the time.
Affected resources (1)
  • Namespace api
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# Validate against your workload's real ingress flows before applying — a bare default-deny
# will drop all ingress until you add explicit allow rules.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:

  namespace: api
spec:

Pod workers/licensed-etl-0

Description

If node ip-10-0-2-a were unavailable, 1 pod(s) running on it would have no remaining node in this reading that satisfies the constraints this model checks. This is a different question from whether a disruption budget would permit the eviction: a budget that allows a pod to leave does not produce anywhere for it to arrive. The model checks a subset of the scheduler's predicates, so it can report that nothing satisfies it and cannot report the opposite — preemption could free room it does not see, and an autoscaler could add nodes this reading does not contain.

Business impact

A node is lost routinely: a spot reclaim, a kernel panic, a node-pool upgrade. The pods listed here are the ones whose declared constraints leave them nothing in the node set as it stands.

Evidence (5)
  • Snapshot taken at 2026-09-15T05:28:50Z. Each resource kind is listed independently, so the node, pod and budget views can differ by moments; re-verify against the live cluster before acting.
  • workers/licensed-etl-0 requests 250m cpu and 512Mi memory; no surviving node in this reading satisfies the modelled constraints
  • a further 1 pod(s) on this node would find no room on the surviving nodes as they are currently packed. That is a capacity observation rather than a constraint, it changes with the next deploy, and this reading discusses aggregate slack in the cost section instead
  • modelled here: the pod's cpu and memory requests against the candidate node's allocatable; nodeSelector, as equality across every key; required node affinity (requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution), over the node's labels; NoSchedule and NoExecute taints against the pod's tolerations; node readiness and the unschedulable flag; a PersistentVolume whose own nodeAffinity pins the pod to a node or a zone
  • not modelled: preemption — a higher-priority pod can evict a lower-priority one and take its place; priorityclasses are not collected; autoscaling — a node pool can add capacity; this reads the node set as it stands; inter-pod affinity and anti-affinity, which are order-dependent; topologySpread skew, which is computed against a domain set that changes as pods are placed; max pods per node, ephemeral-storage and extended resources such as GPUs; per-node volume attach limits (csinodes are not collected); the scheduler's own configuration: which plugins, profiles or extenders are enabled; admission — the pod that would be created from a template is not the pod read here, because injectors add containers and requests
What this does not establish (3)
  • The model checks a SUBSET of the scheduler's predicates, which is what makes the negative sound: a model more permissive than the scheduler finding no fit means the scheduler finds none either. The positive does not follow and is never asserted — that no pod here is listed is not a claim that any pod would be placed.
  • The scheduler's own configuration is unreadable on a managed cluster, admission injects containers into the pod that actually gets placed, and per-node volume-attach limits and max-pods are not read. Preemption is unmodelled.
  • No cost follows from this. Not a node count, not a smaller configuration, not a figure — a pod having nowhere to go says nothing about what the cluster should be sized at.

Enforce a PodSecurity admission profile on namespace api

Namespace api

Description

Namespace api runs workloads but does not enforce a PodSecurity admission profile of baseline or restricted (enforce=<unset>). Without enforcement, the per-container PSS findings in this report describe the spec AS AUTHORED — nothing in the cluster actually blocks a privileged, root, or capability-laden pod from being admitted here. Apply the labels gradually: set warn and audit first to surface what would break, then set enforce. Enforcing restricted on a namespace that already runs noncompliant pods does NOT evict them, but it WILL block the next admission (a redeploy or rollout) — stage it. baseline is the safe first target (it blocks privileged, hostPath, hostNetwork, and host namespaces); however, the per-container findings in this report for this namespace (seccomp, drop-ALL capabilities, allowPrivilegeEscalation, runAsNonRoot) are Restricted-profile controls, so enforce=restricted is required to fully close them — baseline alone will not.

Business impact

PodSecurity admission is the only thing that turns securityContext hardening from a suggestion into a guarantee — without it, a single noncompliant manifest re-opens every gap the per-container checks flag.

  • An admission control governs what may be applied next. It says nothing about what is already running, which was admitted under whatever policy was in force at the time.

SHELL

Description

ClusterRoleBinding acme-everyone-can-read names Group system:authenticated as a subject and points at ClusterRole acme-secret-sync, cluster-wide. system:authenticated is every identity the authenticator accepts, which includes every ServiceAccount in every namespace. This is what the binding says; what any holder of that subject can actually do is the union over every binding that names it, and the absence of a binding is not the absence of the subject: every identity the authenticator accepts belongs to this group, and which identities those are is decided outside the cluster.

system:authenticated is every identity the authenticator accepts, which includes every ServiceAccount in every namespace, so a binding that names it hands the referenced role to everyone it covers at once, without any of them appearing in this or any other object.

  • Whether the grant is reachable was not established. Anonymous requests are accepted or refused by a control-plane flag a managed cluster does not expose, so a binding naming an unauthenticated subject may be live or may be unreachable, and this reading cannot tell those apart.

The label alone is not trusted, because anybody who can create a binding can set it; a labelled binding that is not the upstream one is reported like any other. A binding an installer created without that label is reported even where it is that installer's normal behaviour, because a rule that decided which installers to trust would be making a judgement this reading cannot support.

Namespace workers has no NetworkPolicy — add a default-deny if its CNI enforces policy

Namespace workers

Description

Namespace workers runs 4 workload(s) and defines zero upstream (networking.k8s.io/v1) NetworkPolicy objects. Enforcement of NetworkPolicy depends on the cluster CNI, which could not be confirmed here (a NetworkPolicy is accepted by the API server but silently ignored without an enforcing CNI).   • CNI enforcement of NetworkPolicy could not be confirmed from collected DaemonSets — verify the cluster CNI supports and enforces NetworkPolicy before relying on this remediation
What this does not establish (2)
  • This reports what is not configured, which is not the same as what is not enforced. A CNI may carry segmentation in its own policy objects, which this product does not read, so the absence of an upstream NetworkPolicy is not the absence of isolation.

Affected resources (1)
  • Namespace workers
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# Validate against your workload's real ingress flows before applying — a bare default-deny
# will drop all ingress until you add explicit allow rules.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: workers
spec:
  podSelector: {}  # empty selector = every pod in the namespace
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress

  • What is SERVED is not what is APPLIED. `last-applied-configuration` would be the obvious source for the latter and is refused: it is absent on every GitOps cluster, nothing updates it on a storage migration, and it holds the entire applied manifest.
  • A group/version string is not a stable identity across releases — one API was removed in 1.22 and reintroduced in 1.28 — so the removal schedule is read as a dated dataset with a version and a stamp, not as a permanent fact.
  • Silence from this family means these checks ran and found nothing. It is not a statement that the upgrade will succeed.

Enforce a PodSecurity admission profile on namespace payments

Namespace payments

Description

Namespace payments runs workloads but does not enforce a PodSecurity admission profile of baseline or restricted (enforce=<unset>). Without enforcement, the per-container PSS findings in this report describe the spec AS AUTHORED — nothing in the cluster actually blocks a privileged, root, or capability-laden pod from being admitted here. Apply the labels gradually: set warn and audit first to surface what would break, then set enforce. Enforcing restricted on a namespace that already runs noncompliant pods does NOT evict them, but it WILL block the next admission (a redeploy or rollout) — stage it. baseline is the safe first target (it blocks privileged, hostPath, hostNetwork, and host namespaces); however, the per-container findings in this report for this namespace (seccomp, drop-ALL capabilities, allowPrivilegeEscalation, runAsNonRoot) are Restricted-profile controls, so enforce=restricted is required to fully close them — baseline alone will not.

Business impact

PodSecurity admission is the only thing that turns securityContext hardening from a suggestion into a guarantee — without it, a single noncompliant manifest re-opens every gap the per-container checks flag.

Evidence (1)
  • namespace payments: enforce=<unset>, warn=<unset>, audit=<unset> — admission does not block any pod
What this does not establish (2)
  • This reports what is not configured, which is not the same as what is not enforced. A CNI may carry segmentation in its own policy objects, which this product does not read, so the absence of an upstream NetworkPolicy is not the absence of isolation.
  • An admission control governs what may be applied next. It says nothing about what is already running, which was admitted under whatever policy was in force at the time.
Affected resources (1)
  • Namespace payments
Remediation
Run this command
SHELL 
kubectl label --overwrite namespace payments pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=baseline pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=baseline   # surface breakage first, then set enforce=baseline; use restricted (not baseline) on both warn/audit/enforce to close the per-container seccomp/capabilities/runAsNonRoot findings

Namespace payments has no NetworkPolicy — add a default-deny if its CNI enforces policy

Namespace payments

Description

Namespace payments runs 3 workload(s) and defines zero upstream (networking.k8s.io/v1) NetworkPolicy objects. Enforcement of NetworkPolicy depends on the cluster CNI, which could not be confirmed here (a NetworkPolicy is accepted by the API server but silently ignored without an enforcing CNI). If the CNI enforces policy, start with a default-deny-ingress policy, then add explicit allows for the flows that exist.

Business impact

If the cluster CNI enforces NetworkPolicy, flat pod-to-pod networking lets a single compromised container move laterally across the namespace. If the CNI does not enforce policy (or segments via its own CRDs), this gap may be theoretical — confirm enforcement before relying on it.

Evidence (2)
  • namespace payments: 3 workload(s), 0 networking.k8s.io/v1 NetworkPolicy objects
  • CNI enforcement of NetworkPolicy could not be confirmed from collected DaemonSets — verify the cluster CNI supports and enforces NetworkPolicy before relying on this remediation
What this does not establish (2)
  • This reports what is not configured, which is not the same as what is not enforced. A CNI may carry segmentation in its own policy objects, which this product does not read, so the absence of an upstream NetworkPolicy is not the absence of isolation.
  • An admission control governs what may be applied next. It says nothing about what is already running, which was admitted under whatever policy was in force at the time.
Affected resources (1)
  • Namespace payments
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
# Validate against your workload's real ingress flows before applying — a bare default-deny
# will drop all ingress until you add explicit allow rules.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: payments
spec:
  podSelector: {}  # empty selector = every pod in the namespace
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress

A volume ties payments/payments-ledger-db-0 to zone eu-central-1a

Description

PersistentVolume pvc-ledger-db-0 carries a required nodeAffinity naming zone eu-central-1a, so the pod that mounts it can only run on a node in that zone. The r6i.4xlarge pool (3 node(s)) is priced above at least one instance type of identical vCPU and memory in the same family line. The comparison is between two list prices for the same shape; nothing about the workloads on these nodes is assumed beyond what the tiers below state.

Business impact

Instance types accumulate: a pool created three years ago is still on the type someone chose then, and the catalogue has moved under it. The same machine — same vCPU, same memory, same family — is often listed under a newer name at a lower price, and nothing in the cluster points that out.

Estimated $266/mo ($3,196/yr) at on-demand list pricing.

Evidence (6)
  • Snapshot taken at 2026-09-15T05:28:50Z. Each resource kind is listed independently, so the node, pod and budget views can differ by moments; re-verify against the live cluster before acting.
  • 3 node(s) of r6i.4xlarge in eu-central-1 (on-demand), 16 vCPU · 128 GiB each, list at $887.68/mo per node; the kubelet reports amd64
  • SAME ARCHITECTURE, DIFFERENT VENDOR: r6a.4xlarge lists at $798.91/mo per node — 16 vCPU · 128 GiB on AMD EPYC rather than Intel Xeon, both x86-64, so every image that runs today runs there. Across 3 node(s) that is about $266.30/mo at list. What this does NOT compare is per-vCPU performance: the vCPU counts match, the cores are not the same silicon, and a workload with a vendor-specific dependency (an Intel-only instruction set, a licensed-per-socket product) is the exception this reading cannot see.
  • NOT BANKED: r6g.4xlarge (arm64 Graviton) lists at $710.14/mo per node — 16 vCPU · 128 GiB — which across 3 node(s) WOULD be about $532.61/mo less than today at list. It is not in the figure above because whether this cluster's container images are built for arm64 is a registry fact, and this reading does not touch a registry. If every image is multi-arch, this is the larger saving; if one is not, that workload cannot move. The number is here so you can check; it is not a claim.
  • compared within the same family line only: same extras, same size label, no crossing into local-NVMe ("d"), accelerator (g/p/inf/trn), metal or burst-limited (-flex) variants, because vCPU and memory do not describe those machines
  • both sides are on-demand LIST prices in the same region; a reservation or Savings Plan on the current type is invisible from the cluster and would shrink or erase this difference — that is what --discount models. Whether the proposed type has capacity in your availability zones is not readable here either.
What this does not establish (3)
  • The figure is computed from a dated public list price, not from your bill. No credential of yours was used and no invoice was read, so a negotiated rate, a private offer or a credit is invisible here.
  • Whether a commitment already covers this footprint is a billing-account fact this product cannot see. A saving stated at the on-demand rate is wrong for the term of any plan that already applies.
  • Identified is not realised. Nothing here has been reclaimed, and the arithmetic assumes the freed capacity is actually given up rather than absorbed elsewhere.

Add resource governance to namespace api

Namespace api

Description

Namespace api runs 3 long-running workloads (Deployments/StatefulSets/DaemonSets) with no ResourceQuota and no LimitRange object. There is no namespace-level cap on how much CPU or memory the namespace can claim against the cluster, and no LimitRange to supply default per-container requests. Every observed container already sets explicit requests, so the per-pod gap is limited to the absence of a namespace cap and a default-request safety net for future workloads. Note: this is an object-presence check — defaults injected at admission time by a mutating webhook or policy engine (Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper) are not visible to a read-only scan and may already govern this namespace; verify before acting.

Business impact

A ResourceQuota caps the namespace's total claim against the cluster (capacity planning and blast-radius across namespaces); a LimitRange supplies the per-container default requests that keep pods out of BestEffort. With neither, a co-located namespace has no aggregate ceiling and no default-request safety net.

Evidence (5)
  • namespace api: 3 long-running workloads counted (Deployments/StatefulSets/DaemonSets; Jobs/CronJobs/bare Pods are not counted)
  • namespace api: 0 ResourceQuota objects observed
  • namespace api: 0 LimitRange objects observed
  • all observed containers in this namespace declare explicit CPU/memory requests
  • admission/policy-engine-injected defaults (Kyverno, OPA, mutating webhooks) are not observable in a read-only scan and may already govern this namespace
What this does not establish (2)
  • This reports what is not configured, which is not the same as what is not enforced. A CNI may carry segmentation in its own policy objects, which this product does not read, so the absence of an upstream NetworkPolicy is not the absence of isolation.
  • An admission control governs what may be applied next. It says nothing about what is already running, which was admitted under whatever policy was in force at the time.
Affected resources (1)
  • Namespace api
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: api
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest:   # starting point — right-size from usage before applying
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      default:          # starting point — right-size from usage before applying

Add resource governance to namespace payments

Namespace payments

Description

Namespace payments runs 3 long-running workloads (Deployments/StatefulSets/DaemonSets) with no ResourceQuota and no LimitRange object. There is no namespace-level cap on how much CPU or memory the namespace can claim against the cluster, and no LimitRange to supply default per-container requests. Every observed container already sets explicit requests, so the per-pod gap is limited to the absence of a namespace cap and a default-request safety net for future workloads. Note: this is an object-presence check — defaults injected at admission time by a mutating webhook or policy engine (Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper) are not visible to a read-only scan and may already govern this namespace; verify before acting.

Business impact

A ResourceQuota caps the namespace's total claim against the cluster (capacity planning and blast-radius across namespaces); a LimitRange supplies the per-container default requests that keep pods out of BestEffort. With neither, a co-located namespace has no aggregate ceiling and no default-request safety net.

Evidence (5)
  • namespace payments: 3 long-running workloads counted (Deployments/StatefulSets/DaemonSets; Jobs/CronJobs/bare Pods are not counted)
  • namespace payments: 0 ResourceQuota objects observed
  • namespace payments: 0 LimitRange objects observed
  • all observed containers in this namespace declare explicit CPU/memory requests
  • admission/policy-engine-injected defaults (Kyverno, OPA, mutating webhooks) are not observable in a read-only scan and may already govern this namespace
What this does not establish (2)
  • This reports what is not configured, which is not the same as what is not enforced. A CNI may carry segmentation in its own policy objects, which this product does not read, so the absence of an upstream NetworkPolicy is not the absence of isolation.
  • An admission control governs what may be applied next. It says nothing about what is already running, which was admitted under whatever policy was in force at the time.
Affected resources (1)
  • Namespace payments
Remediation
Apply this manifest
YAML 
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: payments
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest:   # starting point — right-size from usage before applying
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      default:          # starting point — right-size from usage before applying
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi

Node pool m6i.xlarge: up to 2 node(s) of request-slack — verify usage before reclaiming

Node ip-10-0-1-a

+8 more resources
Description

Node pool m6i.xlarge (9 × m6i.xlarge) shows 2 node(s) of AGGREGATE slack between summed pod requests (DaemonSet pods excluded) and allocatable capacity. This is an upper-bound ceiling, not a drainable count: it is requests-only and is NOT a safe basis for removing nodes — pods that request less than they use will OOM when packed onto fewer nodes, the autoscaler gates on the same requests, and the figure assumes free repacking it never verifies (it does not model PDBs, anti-affinity/topology-spread, or bin-packing fragmentation). Treat it as a candidate to INVESTIGATE with real utilisation (connect Prometheus), not a realisable saving — the dollar impact here is 0 until usage confirms the headroom.

Business impact

Over-provisioned nodes bill full price — but reclaiming them safely requires confirming real usage is below requests; acting on request-slack alone risks an OOM outage.

Evidence (6)
  • pool m6i.xlarge (9 nodes): summed pod REQUESTS 24.4 CPU / 94.7Gi (DaemonSet pods excluded) vs allocatable 35.1 CPU / 135.0Gi -> 2 node(s) of aggregate request-slack
  • REQUESTS-ONLY, not live usage: if pods request less CPU/memory than they actually consume, packing this pool onto fewer nodes will OOM/evict at runtime — and the cluster-autoscaler, which gates on the same requests, would drain straight into it. Do NOT remove nodes on this signal alone.
  • AGGREGATE CEILING, not a drainable count: this number is total-unused-capacity divided by per-node-capacity — it assumes every remaining request can be freely repacked onto the survivors. It does NOT model per-node bin-packing fragmentation (many pods that each fit the slack but collectively don't), PodDisruptionBudgets that block the eviction draining requires, or pod anti-affinity / topologySpreadConstraints that pin one replica per node. Real reclaimable nodes are at most this many and often fewer; treat it as an upper limit to investigate.
  • Verify before acting: connect Prometheus (--prometheus-url) so the usage-based Rightsizing rule sizes requests to real p95 usage — the safe path to reclaiming capacity.
  • UNVERIFIED upper bound, only if usage is at or below requests: region eu-central-1 m6i.xlarge about $167.90/node/mo × 2, about $335.80/mo — NOT counted in savings until real usage confirms it.
  • HA floor: this suggestion already leaves at least 2 nodes (dropping below 2 removes failure-domain redundancy and rolling-update headroom). Before reclaiming, confirm this pool isn't the cluster's DNS/ingress tier or home to a single-AZ-pinned / single-replica critical workload — none of which is distinguishable from request data alone.
What this does not establish (1)
  • The dollar impact is zero on purpose. This is a candidate to investigate with real utilisation, not a saving: requests-only slack cannot tell an idle pool from one whose pods under-request against what they actually use, and acting on the second packs a cluster into an OOM.

CronJob workers/acme-nightly-reconcile sets no startingDeadlineSeconds

CronJob workers/acme-nightly-reconcile

Description

CronJob workers/acme-nightly-reconcile leaves spec.startingDeadlineSeconds unset. The controller then has no bound on how late a missed run may start: after an outage it counts every schedule it missed, and past a hundred it stops scheduling the CronJob entirely until the next window. With the deadline set, runs older than it are skipped and the count never accumulates.

Business impact

This is a field that costs nothing while everything works and decides what happens after a control-plane outage — which is exactly when nobody is reading CronJob specs. Whether this cluster has ever hit it is not readable from a snapshot.

9 m6i.xlarge node(s) run on-demand where a Savings Plan is published

Node ip-10-0-1-a

+7 more resources
Description

The m6i.xlarge pool (9 node(s)) is billed at on-demand list. AWS publishes a Compute Savings Plan rate for this type in this region; the evidence states what the pool would cost under it and the two conditions under which that figure is real. Nothing is counted toward the headline.

Business impact

On-demand is the price of not having decided. A pool that has run unchanged for a year has paid the list premium for a year; a pool created last week has not, and the snapshot cannot tell the two apart — which is why this states the difference and declines to sum it.

Evidence (6)
  • Snapshot taken at 2026-09-15T05:28:50Z. Each resource kind is listed independently, so the node, pod and budget views can differ by moments; re-verify against the live cluster before acting.
  • 9 on-demand node(s) of m6i.xlarge in eu-central-1, list $167.90/mo each ($1,511.10/mo for the pool)
  • 1yr No Upfront: $0.1754/h per node — $1,152.18/mo for the pool against $1,511.10 at list, 24% less
  • 3yr No Upfront: $0.1196/h per node — $785.97/mo for the pool against $1,511.10 at list, 48% less
  • NOT BANKED, AND NOT BECAUSE IT COULD NOT BE PRICED. This reading is one moment; a commitment is one or three years. Whether this footprint held last month or will hold next month is not in the snapshot — the app's past readings are where that is checked — and whether a plan already covers these nodes is a billing-account fact no cluster object carries. Both must be true before the difference above is a saving; until then it is the price of a decision, stated so you can make it.
  • rate: Compute Savings Plan, the flexible and least-discounting plan AWS sells; an EC2 Instance Savings Plan on this family would discount more and commit harder. Linux, shared tenancy, list prices in this region.
What this does not establish (3)
  • The figure is computed from a dated public list price, not from your bill. No credential of yours was used and no invoice was read, so a negotiated rate, a private offer or a credit is invisible here.
  • Whether a commitment already covers this footprint is a billing-account fact this product cannot see. A saving stated at the on-demand rate is wrong for the term of any plan that already applies.
  • Identified is not realised. Nothing here has been reclaimed, and the arithmetic assumes the freed capacity is actually given up rather than absorbed elsewhere.

info config Open

3 LoadBalancer Service(s) set externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster

Service payments/legacy-checkout-lb

+2 more resources
Description

3 LoadBalancer Service(s) explicitly set externalTrafficPolicy to Cluster. kube-proxy then forwards to a backend on any node and source-NATs the second hop, so every backend sees a node address rather than the client's. Load spreads evenly, which is what the setting buys.

Business impact

Anything that reasons about the client address — rate limiting, geo-routing, allow-lists, audit logs — sees a node instead. The application is usually written before the Service and never told.

Evidence (4)
  • Snapshot taken at 2026-09-15T05:28:50Z. Each resource kind is listed independently, so the node, pod and budget views can differ by moments; re-verify against the live cluster before acting.
  • Services explicitly setting Cluster: payments/legacy-checkout-lb, payments/legacy-payments-lb, payments/old-admin-lb
  • an UNSET policy is Cluster by default and is not reported here — that would be reporting Kubernetes rather than this cluster
  • the alternative, Local, preserves the client address and blackholes requests arriving at a node with no local backend; neither setting is a default to prefer
What this does not establish (2)
  • This is a state read at one instant. The snapshot has no time axis, so nothing here is a rate, a trend or a duration — a restart count is a total the kubelet reports, not a frequency.
  • No cause is asserted. The reading records what the cluster says about itself; why it says it is outside what a read-only client can see.
Affected resources (3)
  • Service payments/legacy-checkout-lb
  • Service payments/legacy-payments-lb
  • Service payments/old-admin-lb

Whether the cluster actually enforces a profile is a separate signal — see the PodSecurity admission check (rule k8s.namespace.pss-admission-not-enforced), which reports what admission blocks. Read the two together: a spec can omit a field that admission or a mutating webhook would otherwise reject.

NSA/CISA Hardening Guidance (informational mapping)

Guidance, not a certifiable control catalog. The rows above (framework NSA-CISA) map observations to hardening sections. The areas below are structurally out of reach for a read-only API client and are listed explicitly so this mapping is never mistaken for full coverage.

Not covered (manual)

  • Audit Logging & Threat Detection (entire section) — Audit policy is an apiserver flag + provider log sink, and threat detection is a runtime/SIEM concern (Falco, etc.) — none observable from a read-only object API. Route to your logging/SIEM stack.
  • Network Separation — control-plane exposure, etcd/API TLS, secrets-at-rest — Provider-internal on managed clusters (EKS/AKS/GKE). The control-plane network posture and encryption config are not exposed by the object API.
  • Authentication & Authorization — anonymous-auth, OIDC, static tokens, kubeconfig hygiene — These live in apiserver flags and the external IdP, not in API objects. Verify against your provider config and identity provider.
  • Upgrading & Application Security — version currency, patching, vulnerability scanning — Image hygiene is partially covered (mutable-tag mapping); full coverage needs EOL/version data and an image scanner (Trivy/Grype). Run a scanner in CI.

    Set resource requests on workers/risk-batch-processor

    Containers with no effective request (no explicit request, no limit defaulting, no namespace LimitRange) land in BestEffort QoS: the scheduler can't bin-pack them safely and the kubelet evicts them first under pressure. Note: a limit alone, or a namespace LimitRange defaultRequest, already supplies an effective request — those cases are NOT flagged here.

    low effort F-FD12DA5D9579

Appendix

Every derived figure in this report traces back to the pricing table, assumptions and confidence ranges below.

The pricing basis behind the dollar math, the assumptions the conclusions rest on, and the per-finding confidence model — so nothing on the cover or in the reconciliation is taken on faith.

Pricing table AWS on-demand list · eu-central-1 · as of 2026-09

List-price basis for every priced node pool. Subtotals sum to the compute figure underlying the cluster bill; reserved / savings-plan rates land below this.

Instance typeSpecCount$/node-moSubtotal/mo
m6i.xlarge 4 vCPU · 16 GiB 9 $167.90 $1,511.10
r6i.4xlarge 4 vCPU · 16 GiB 3 $887.68 $2,663.04
Compute subtotal 12 — $4,174.14/mo

Assumptions & confidence

The four assumptions every figure in this audit rests on. Footnote 1 is the one the cover and reconciliation cite directly.

  1. Cost basis. Cluster spend covers compute (priced node pools) plus EKS control-plane and best-effort NLB base charges and EBS / persistent-volume storage, summed from PV and PVC capacity at list per GB-month ($202/mo), totalling $4,509/mo. Cross-AZ data transfer is not collected and is excluded — true spend is therefore at or above this figure, never below it.
  2. Savings figures are estimates. Every dollar uses AWS on-demand list pricing as of 2026-09. Organisations on reservations or savings plans should expect lower realised numbers; treat the headline as an upper-bound list-price estimate, not a guaranteed return.
  3. Per-finding confidence. Each finding carries a confidence value shown on its card. Hand-crafted v0 findings default high; lower values flag observations that warrant manual confirmation before action.
  4. Compliance is observational. Control rows are observations mapped to framework controls, not an audit opinion. Review flagged rows with your QSA / auditor.

If a figure in this report is wrong

This document is a measurement, and a measurement can be wrong. The tool that produced it contacts no service of ours, so nothing about this run reached anybody: there is no telemetry to look at and nothing has been reported anywhere.

Run shoalcheck support --input <report.json>. It writes a few kilobytes of JSON carrying the binary's version and platform, counts, which of the tool's own rule ids fired, and the cause recorded for any resource kind the run did not get back. It carries no cluster name, no region, no namespace, workload, node, service or hostname, and nothing from any finding — not redacted, absent. Read the file before sending it; it is short, and it says what it contains.

— End of audit · Shoalcheck · Confidential —
